This guide follows [`Workshop_Week09_SLR.qmd`](Workshop_Week09_SLR.qmd).
It contains the completed code and interpretations for the workbook.

For the first part of this course we focused on working with data in R and RStudio,
including using `ggplot2` to explore and visualise relationships. More recently we
have looked at probability distributions, sampling variation and the central limit
theorem, which give us a way to think about uncertainty in estimates from data.

In this workshop we start bringing those ideas together. We will use plots to explore
relationships between vehicle characteristics and fuel use, then fit our first regression
models to describe those relationships numerically. Along the way we will interpret the fitted line, coefficients, $R^2$, predictions
and residuals. Then we ask how uncertain the fitted line is, and whether its
assumptions are believable.

[Waka Kotahi's vehicle-fleet data](https://www.nzta.govt.nz/resources/new-zealand-motor-vehicle-register-statistics/new-zealand-vehicle-fleet-open-data-sets)
provide a snapshot of vehicles recorded on the Motor Vehicle Register, while
[EECA's guide to vehicle energy-economy labels](https://www.eeca.govt.nz/regulations/vehicle-emissions-and-energy-economy-labelling-programme/about-the-vehicle-emissions-and-energy-economy-labelling-programme/)
explains the standard fuel-economy measure in litres per 100 km. The supplied
extract contains 467 unique vehicle specifications, prepared from Waka Kotahi's
vehicle-fleet data as at **31 July 2026** and containing model-year 2025 petrol
passenger cars and vans with complete measurements.
Download the supplied extract here: [2025 cars dataset](https://knowlton.co.nz/297101/labs/nz_vehicles_2025.csv).

## Today's question

How much can one vehicle specification tell us about fuel use?

## Learning objectives

By the end of this workshop you should be able to:

- recognise an approximately linear association from a scatterplot;
- fit and interpret a simple linear regression model;
- interpret the slope, intercept and $R^2$;
- calculate and interpret a fitted value;
- define and interpret a residual;
- interpret the standard error, 95% confidence interval and p-value for a slope;
- distinguish a confidence interval for an average from a prediction interval
  for one vehicle; and
- use residual plots to check the L-I-N-E assumptions and screen for
  influential observations.

## 1. Explore engine size and power

**What to do:** Start by looking at the data before fitting a model. For each
scatterplot, describe the direction, strength and shape of the relationship and
look for anything unusual. Then calculate the correlation and ask whether a
straight line looks like a reasonable summary.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tibble)
library(broom)

vehicles <- read_csv("https://knowlton.co.nz/297101/labs/nz_vehicles_2025.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
glimpse(vehicles)
```

Each row is one unique 2025 petrol vehicle specification. Fuel use is the
combined-cycle test value in litres per 100 km, so the plots describe
associations among specifications rather than causal effects or real-world
consumption.

### Demonstration: engine size

Let's start with the flexible smoother we learned earlier in the course to get a feel
for the relationship between engine size and fuel use. A reminder that this
lets us look at the *shape* of the relationship first and decide whether a linear
model is a reasonable summary.

```{r}
ggplot(vehicles, aes(engine_l, fuel_use_l_per_100km)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = "Engine size (litres)",
    y = "Combined fuel use (L/100 km)",
    title = "Do larger engines tend to use more fuel?"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

vehicles |>
  summarise(engine_correlation = cor(engine_l, fuel_use_l_per_100km))
```

Look at the scatterplot first. Describe the direction, shape and strength of
the relationship, and note anything unusual. Then use the correlation to
summarise its linear strength. Does that number support what you saw? Remember
that correlation has no units and is not a slope.

The relationship is positive, strong and approximately linear. The correlation
is about 0.90, so larger engines tend to be associated with higher fuel use,
although there is still visible vehicle-to-vehicle variation. Correlation is
unit-free and measures linear strength; it is not the slope and does not imply
that changing engine size causes the difference. Correlation only summarises
linear association, so always look at the scatterplot as well. Non-linearity,
unusual observations or other structure can be hidden by a single correlation
value.

### Your turn: engine power

Repeat the same process for engine power. Before looking at the correlation, use
the plot to decide whether the relationship is positive or negative, whether it
looks approximately linear, and whether it appears stronger or weaker than the
engine-size relationship.

**Hint:** Use `ggplot()` with a LOESS smooth, then calculate the correlation
with `cor()`.

```{r}
ggplot(vehicles, aes(power_kw, fuel_use_l_per_100km)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = "Engine power (kW)",
    y = "Combined fuel use (L/100 km)",
    title = "Do more powerful vehicles tend to use more fuel?"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

vehicles |>
  summarise(power_correlation = cor(power_kw, fuel_use_l_per_100km))
```

Power also has a positive relationship with fuel use. Its correlation is about
0.884, slightly smaller than the engine-size correlation in this dataset. Again,
the correlation should be interpreted alongside the scatterplot because it only
summarises the linear part of the relationship.

Both relationships are positive and approximately linear. The engine-size
relationship appears slightly more nearly linear in this dataset, and it has the
larger correlation (0.901 versus 0.884). These correlations measure unit-free
linear strength; they are not slopes and should not be compared as changes in
fuel use per unit of the predictor.

Which relationship appears more nearly linear? Which has the stronger linear
association according to correlation? Use the plot and correlation as evidence;
do not interpret either correlation as a slope.

## 2. Fit simple linear models

**What to do:** Fit a simple linear regression model with fuel use as the
response and engine size as the explanatory variable. Identify the intercept and
slope, then add the fitted regression line to the scatterplot. Repeat the same
process using engine power.

You have now examined the shape of the relationship. We will fit a
straight-line model and compare it with the pattern you saw in the data.

A simple linear model describes the average response as a straight-line
function of one explanatory variable:

$$
\widehat{y} = \widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 x.
$$

```{r}
engine_model <- lm(
  fuel_use_l_per_100km ~ engine_l,
  data = vehicles
)

engine_model
```

```{r}
ggplot(vehicles, aes(engine_l, fuel_use_l_per_100km)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = "Engine size (litres)",
    y = "Combined fuel use (L/100 km)",
    title = "A straight-line model for engine size and fuel use"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

From the printed model, identify the intercept and slope. On the plot, check
whether the fitted line follows the main pattern in the points. What does the
line represent for vehicles with the same engine size?

There are many possible straight lines we could draw through these data.
`lm()` uses least squares: it chooses the intercept and slope that minimise the
sum of the squared vertical distances between the observed values and the fitted
line. This is the same idea as minimising the mean squared error we looked at
previously.

What is `lm()` changing when it searches for the best-fitting line?

It changes the intercept and slope. The least-squares search chooses the values
that minimise the sum of the squared residuals, so the resulting line is the
closest straight-line summary under that criterion.

The fitted line captures the main increasing pattern, while individual vehicles
remain above and below it. It is a summary of the conditional mean, not an exact
rule.

### Your turn: power model

Fit the power model yourself before looking at the answer. Compare its fitted
line with the LOESS smooth from Section 1. Does a straight line still seem like
a reasonable summary?

**Hint:** Fit fuel use as the response and `power_kw` as the explanatory
variable with `lm()`. Add a straight fitted line to a scatterplot with
`geom_smooth(method = "lm")`.

```{r}
power_model <- lm(
  fuel_use_l_per_100km ~ power_kw,
  data = vehicles
)

power_model
```

```{r}
ggplot(vehicles, aes(power_kw, fuel_use_l_per_100km)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = "Engine power (kW)",
    y = "Combined fuel use (L/100 km)",
    title = "A straight-line model for engine power and fuel use"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

Both lines capture a positive average association and leave meaningful
vehicle-specific variation unexplained. The straight line is a reasonable
summary for the power relationship, although it is not an exact rule for every
vehicle.

## 3. Coefficients and R²

**What to do:** Use `coef()` to examine the fitted coefficients. Identify the
intercept and slope, and interpret the slope in the units of the problem rather
than just reporting the number. Then use $R^2$ to describe how much of the
observed variation in fuel use is accounted for by the model.

```{r}
engine_coefficients <- coef(engine_model)
engine_coefficients
```

The fitted engine-size slope is 1.886 L/100 km per litre, so a one-litre
difference in engine size is associated with an average difference of about
1.89 L/100 km in fuel use.

The fitted equation is approximately

$$
\widehat{\text{fuel use}} = 4.070 + 1.886(\text{engine size})
$$

Write the fitted equation. Identify the intercept and slope, then interpret the
slope in L/100 km per litre of engine size. Before giving the intercept a
practical meaning, check whether zero litres is represented in these data.

A one-litre difference in engine size is associated with about 1.886 L/100 km
higher average fuel use. Zero litres is outside the observed range (0.998 to
6.749 L), so the intercept is a mathematical line value rather than a practical
vehicle prediction.

We already calculated the correlation between engine size and fuel use. Square
it and compare it with the model $R^2$. What do you notice? Write one sentence
about how much variation the engine-size model explains.

**Hint:** Compare the squared correlation with
`glance(engine_model)$r.squared`.

```{r}
engine_r <- cor(vehicles$engine_l, vehicles$fuel_use_l_per_100km)
tibble(
  correlation = engine_r,
  correlation_squared = engine_r^2,
  r_squared = glance(engine_model)$r.squared,
  difference = correlation_squared - r_squared
)
```

The correlation is about 0.901 and the simple-model R-squared is about 0.812.
Thus the engine-size model accounts for roughly 81% of the observed variation
in fuel use in this dataset. For simple linear regression with an intercept,
$R^2 = r^2$. Here $0.901^2\approx0.812$, which is exactly the $R^2$ from
the fitted model. This equivalence holds for simple linear regression with an
intercept. Once we move to multiple regression next week, there is no single
correlation that we can simply square to obtain the model $R^2$.

### Power coefficients and fit

```{r}
power_coefficients <- coef(power_model)
power_fit <- glance(power_model)

power_coefficients
power_fit |>
  select(r.squared)
```

Now interpret the power model yourself. What does the slope mean in L/100 km
per kW? Is that a useful scale, or would reporting the change per 100 kW be
easier to understand? Compare its $R^2$ with the engine-size model and state
which model accounts for more of the observed variation.

The power slope is about 0.0186 L/100 km per kW, or about 1.86 L/100 km per
100 kW. The fitted equation is approximately

$$
\widehat{\text{fuel use}} = 4.705 + 0.0186(\text{power}) .
$$

Power has an R-squared of about 0.782, compared with about 0.812 for engine
size. In these data, the engine-size model therefore accounts for slightly more
of the observed variation in fuel use.

## 4. Make a prediction

**What to do:** Use the fitted equation to calculate the fitted fuel use for a
vehicle with a 2.0 L engine by hand. Then use `predict()` to obtain the same
value in R. The two answers should agree. Explain what the fitted value
represents and whether it describes every individual vehicle with a 2.0 L
engine.

**Hint:** Use the intercept and engine-size slope from `coef(engine_model)`;
for the R prediction, supply a one-row tibble with `engine_l = 2`.

```{r}
engine_prediction_manual <- coef(engine_model)[["(Intercept)"]] +
  coef(engine_model)[["engine_l"]] * 2

engine_prediction_r <- predict(
  engine_model,
  newdata = tibble(engine_l = 2)
)

tibble(
  manual = engine_prediction_manual,
  using_predict = as.numeric(engine_prediction_r),
  difference = manual - using_predict
)
```

The predicted average fuel use for a 2.0 L vehicle is about 7.84 L/100 km. The
manual and `predict()` values agree. This is the fitted mean fuel use for
vehicles with a 2.0 L engine according to this model. Note that individual 2.0 L
vehicles can sit well above or below this value, so it should
not be interpreted as *truth* or a guarantee for an individual vehicle.

What does your fitted value represent? Does the model say that every 2.0 L
vehicle will have this fuel use?

It is the model’s estimated mean fuel use for vehicles with a 2.0 L engine. It
does not mean every 2.0 L vehicle will use 7.84 L/100 km; individual vehicles
can be above or below this fitted value.

## 5. What is a residual?

A residual is the difference between what we observed and what the model fitted:

$$
e_i = y_i-\hat{y}_i
$$

A positive residual means the observed fuel use was above the fitted value; a
negative residual means it was below.

**What to do:** Use `augment()` to compare the observed fuel use, fitted value
and residual for several vehicles. Check that

$$
\text{residual}=\text{observed}-\text{fitted}.
$$

Find one positive residual and one negative residual and explain what each means
in the context of fuel use.

**Hint:** In the augmented results, the observed response is
`fuel_use_l_per_100km`, the fitted value is `.fitted`, and the residual is
`.resid`.

```{r}
engine_results <- augment(engine_model)
engine_results |>
  select(engine_l, fuel_use_l_per_100km, .fitted, .resid) |>
  slice_head(n = 8)
```

On the plot, the residual is the vertical distance from each observed value to
the fitted line. Before looking at the residual column, use the graph to decide
whether a point should have a positive or negative residual.

Use the plot to find one point above the fitted line and one below it. Predict
the sign of each residual from the graph, then check those signs in the table.
What are the units of a residual?

**Hint:** The residual is the observed value minus the fitted value.

```{r}
set.seed(297101)
engine_gap_data <- engine_results |>
  slice_sample(n = min(30, nrow(engine_results)))

ggplot(vehicles, aes(engine_l, fuel_use_l_per_100km)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_line(
    data = engine_results |> arrange(engine_l),
    aes(y = .fitted),
    colour = "#2C7FB8",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    data = engine_gap_data,
    aes(xend = engine_l, yend = .fitted),
    colour = "#D95F02",
    alpha = 0.65
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Engine size (litres)",
    y = "Combined fuel use (L/100 km)",
    title = "Observed values and their fitted values"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

In the displayed table, the first vehicle has a residual of about -1.73 L/100
km: it uses less fuel than the fitted value for its engine size. The fourth
vehicle has a residual of about +0.62 L/100 km: it uses more fuel than the
fitted value. The sign comes from observed minus fitted, not from the size of
the engine itself.

A near-zero average residual is expected from least squares, but it does not by
itself establish that the model is adequate. We check the model properly in
Section 8.

Each residual is in L/100 km. A point above the line has a positive residual;
one below has a negative residual. The residual is vertical because the model
predicts the response at the observed explanatory value. When an intercept is
included in the model, least squares makes the mean residual essentially zero,
but that algebraic fact does not validate the model.

## 6. How uncertain is the slope?

**What to do:** These estimates come from one set of vehicle specifications.
Use the coefficient table to read the standard error, 95% confidence interval
and p-value for the slope. State the null hypothesis being tested and keep
statistical evidence separate from practical importance and causality.

If we had a different, comparable set of vehicles, we would get a slightly
different fitted slope. The **standard error** estimates how much the slope
would vary across those samples. The t statistic is the estimate divided by its
standard error, and the p-value tests $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$, no linear relationship
in the population.

### Demonstration: the engine-size slope

```{r}
summary(engine_model)
engine_tidy <- tidy(engine_model, conf.int = TRUE)
engine_tidy
```

```{r}
#| include: false
engine_row <- engine_tidy |> filter(term == "engine_l")
```

Find the engine-size row. For this test, $H_0:\beta_{\mathrm{engine}}=0$ and
$H_A:\beta_{\mathrm{engine}}\ne0$. Does the 95% confidence interval include
zero, and does that agree with the p-value? Interpret the interval in
L/100 km per litre.

The slope is `r round(engine_row$estimate, 3)` L/100 km per litre with a
standard error of `r round(engine_row$std.error, 3)`, so
$t = `r round(engine_row$statistic, 1)`$: the estimate is about 45 standard
errors from zero. The p-value is far below 0.05, so the data give very strong
evidence against a zero slope. The 95% confidence interval,
`r round(engine_row$conf.low, 2)` to `r round(engine_row$conf.high, 2)`
L/100 km per litre, excludes zero, which agrees with the test. Under
repeated-sampling reasoning, values in that range are compatible with these
data and the model.

That evidence is about a linear association among these specifications. It
does not show that enlarging an engine causes higher fuel use, and it says
nothing yet about whether the model's assumptions hold. Section 8 checks that.

A p-value is calculated assuming the null and the model are true. It is not the
probability that the null is true, and a large p-value never proves the null.

### Your turn: the power slope

Use `tidy()` with `conf.int = TRUE` on `power_model`. Interpret the power
slope's 95% confidence interval per 100 kW, and state the null hypothesis and
your conclusion.

```{r}
power_row <- tidy(power_model, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(term == "power_kw")

power_row |>
  mutate(across(c(estimate, conf.low, conf.high), \(x) 100 * x,
                .names = "{.col}_per_100kW")) |>
  select(estimate_per_100kW, conf.low_per_100kW, conf.high_per_100kW, p.value)
```

$H_0:\beta_{\mathrm{power}}=0$. Per 100 kW, the slope is about
`r round(100 * power_row$estimate, 2)` L/100 km, with a 95% confidence interval
of `r round(100 * power_row$conf.low, 2)` to
`r round(100 * power_row$conf.high, 2)` L/100 km. The interval excludes zero and
the p-value is tiny, so we reject a zero power slope. Rescaling to 100 kW
changes the units of the slope and interval, not the evidence: the t statistic
and p-value are the same.

## 7. The average vehicle or one vehicle?

**What to do:** Use `predict()` to calculate both intervals for a vehicle with a
2.0 L engine. Compare their widths and explain why they differ.

A **confidence interval** describes uncertainty about the *average* fuel use of
all 2.0 L vehicles. A **prediction interval** describes where *one new* 2.0 L
vehicle's fuel use might fall, so it also includes the vehicle-to-vehicle
variation around the line.

### Demonstration: confidence interval for the average

```{r}
new_vehicle <- tibble(engine_l = 2)

predict(engine_model, newdata = new_vehicle, interval = "confidence")
```

### Your turn: prediction interval for one vehicle

Calculate a prediction interval for one vehicle with a 2.0 L engine. Which
interval is wider, by roughly how much, and why?

**Hint:** Use `interval = "prediction"`.

```{r}
engine_ci <- predict(engine_model, newdata = new_vehicle, interval = "confidence")
engine_pi <- predict(engine_model, newdata = new_vehicle, interval = "prediction")
engine_pi

tibble(
  interval = c("Confidence: average 2.0 L vehicle", "Prediction: one 2.0 L vehicle"),
  width = c(engine_ci[, "upr"] - engine_ci[, "lwr"], engine_pi[, "upr"] - engine_pi[, "lwr"])
)
```

Both intervals are centred on the same fitted value,
`r round(engine_ci[, "fit"], 2)` L/100 km. The confidence interval for the
average 2.0 L vehicle is only about
`r round(engine_ci[, "upr"] - engine_ci[, "lwr"], 2)` L/100 km wide, because
with 467 vehicles the line's height at 2.0 L is estimated precisely. The
prediction interval for one vehicle runs from `r round(engine_pi[, "lwr"], 1)`
to `r round(engine_pi[, "upr"], 1)` L/100 km, about
`r round((engine_pi[, "upr"] - engine_pi[, "lwr"]) / (engine_ci[, "upr"] - engine_ci[, "lwr"]))`
times wider. It adds the scatter of individual vehicles around the line
(residual SD about `r round(sigma(engine_model), 2)` L/100 km), and collecting
more data cannot remove that scatter.

## 8. Check the L-I-N-E assumptions

**What to do:** Every standard error, p-value and interval above assumed L-I-N-E.
Work through the assumptions one at a time for the engine-size model. For each
one, say what pattern would be reassuring, what you actually see, and whether it
matters. Departures happen in degrees; they are not pass/fail rules.

### Demonstration: L and E, residuals against fitted values

```{r}
plot(engine_model, which = 1)
```

If the straight line is the right shape, the residuals scatter evenly around
zero with no curve. If the spread is constant, the vertical scatter stays about
the same width from left to right.

### Your turn: linearity and equal variance

Look at the red trend line and the width of the cloud. Is there a curve the line
has missed? Does the spread change as the fitted values increase? Then check
the spread again with the scale-location plot.

```{r}
plot(engine_model, which = 3)
```

**Linearity:** The trend line stays near zero for most fitted values, then bends
downwards above about 13 L/100 km. The vehicles with the largest engines tend to
use less fuel than the straight line predicts, so the line overstates fuel use
at the top end. It is a mild departure affecting a small number of vehicles,
but predictions for very large engines deserve caution.

**Equal variance:** The residual cloud is a little narrower at low fitted values
than at high ones, and the scale-location trend rises gently. The spread grows
modestly, so a single prediction-interval width will be slightly too wide for
small engines and slightly too narrow for large ones.

### Demonstration: I, independence comes from the design

No plot of these residuals can show independence. Each row is a unique vehicle
specification, but several rows are variants of the same make and model, often
sharing an engine.

### Your turn: independence

Why might two variants of the same model have related residuals? What would you
want to know about how this dataset was built?

Variants of the same model (for example a coupe and convertible with the same
engine) share engineering and are tested in similar ways, so if one sits above
the line, its sibling probably does too. That is dependence: the 467 rows carry
less independent information than 467 unrelated vehicles, and the standard
errors are likely a bit too small. We would want to know how many distinct
models and engines there are, and how the extract decided which variants count
as unique specifications.

### Demonstration: N, the Q-Q plot

```{r}
plot(engine_model, which = 2)
```

If the residuals were normal, the points would follow the dashed line. Look at
the centre first, then the tails.

### Your turn: normality

Where do the residuals depart from the line? Are those departures in the
centre or in the tails, and are they on one side?

The centre follows the line closely. The departures are mainly in the upper
tail, which bends above the line: there are
more vehicles with large positive residuals (much higher fuel use than the line
predicts) than a normal distribution would give. With 467 vehicles, the slope's
confidence interval is not much affected by this, but a prediction interval for
one vehicle relies more directly on the residual shape, so its upper limit may
be too low.

### Demonstration: influence

```{r}
plot(engine_model, which = 5)

engine_influence <- augment(engine_model, data = vehicles) |>
  slice_max(.cooksd, n = 5) |>
  select(make, model, body_type, engine_l, fuel_use_l_per_100km, .cooksd)

engine_influence
```

Cook's distance measures how much the fitted line would move if that vehicle
were left out. A large value is a reason to check the record, not to delete it.

### Your turn: investigate influence

Which vehicles have the largest Cook's distances? Are they unusual in engine
size, in fuel use, or both? Would you remove any of them? Why or why not?

The largest Cook's distances belong to large-engined sports cars and SUVs,
mostly Chevrolet Corvette variants. Their engines are at the top of the
observed range (which gives them leverage), and their fuel use is well above or
below the line for that engine size. Even the largest value,
`r round(max(engine_influence$.cooksd), 2)`, is small: removing that vehicle
would barely move the line. These are genuine vehicles, so there is no reason
to delete them. They do reinforce the linearity point: the largest engines are
where the straight line fits least well.

## 9. Independent workflow: gross vehicle mass

**Complete the full workflow using gross vehicle mass.**

1. Plot gross mass against fuel use with a smooth. Describe the direction,
   strength and shape, and calculate the correlation.
2. Fit and print a simple model called `mass_model`. Interpret its slope per
   1000 kg and decide whether the intercept has a useful practical meaning.
3. Report $R^2$ and explain how much variation the model accounts for.
4. Report the 95% confidence interval and p-value for the slope, per 1000 kg.
5. Predict fuel use at 2000 kg with both a confidence interval and a prediction
   interval, and compare their widths.
6. Work through L-I-N-E and influence for `mass_model`. Which assumption
   concerns you most, and how does it affect the intervals you just calculated?
7. Compare this model's $R^2$ with the engine-size and power models. Which
   single-predictor model accounts for the most variation in this dataset?

```{r}
ggplot(vehicles, aes(gross_mass_kg, fuel_use_l_per_100km)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = "Gross mass (kg)",
    y = "Combined fuel use (L/100 km)",
    title = "Gross mass and fuel use"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

mass_correlation <- cor(vehicles$gross_mass_kg, vehicles$fuel_use_l_per_100km)
mass_model <- lm(
  fuel_use_l_per_100km ~ gross_mass_kg,
  data = vehicles
)
mass_coefficients <- coef(mass_model)
mass_fit <- glance(mass_model)
mass_prediction <- predict(
  mass_model,
  newdata = tibble(gross_mass_kg = 2000)
)

tibble(
  correlation = mass_correlation,
  r_squared = mass_fit$r.squared,
  slope_per_1000_kg = 1000 * unname(mass_coefficients["gross_mass_kg"]),
  predicted_fuel_use_at_2000_kg = as.numeric(mass_prediction)
)
```

Gross mass has a positive association with fuel use, but its single-predictor
R-squared is only about 0.331. The slope is about 3.29 L/100 km per 1000 kg.
The model predicts about 8.25 L/100 km at 2000 kg. Of the three single-predictor
models considered here, engine size has the highest in-sample R-squared. A
larger R-squared does not make a relationship causal. It only tells us that the
fitted model accounts for a larger proportion of the observed variation in the
response in this dataset.

```{r}
mass_row <- tidy(mass_model, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(term == "gross_mass_kg")

mass_row |>
  mutate(across(c(estimate, conf.low, conf.high), \(x) 1000 * x,
                .names = "{.col}_per_1000kg")) |>
  select(estimate_per_1000kg, conf.low_per_1000kg, conf.high_per_1000kg, p.value)

new_mass <- tibble(gross_mass_kg = 2000)
mass_ci <- predict(mass_model, newdata = new_mass, interval = "confidence")
mass_pi <- predict(mass_model, newdata = new_mass, interval = "prediction")
mass_ci
mass_pi
```

The 95% confidence interval for the slope is
`r round(1000 * mass_row$conf.low, 2)` to `r round(1000 * mass_row$conf.high, 2)`
L/100 km per 1000 kg, and the p-value is tiny, so there is strong evidence of a
positive linear association. A low $R^2$ and strong evidence for a non-zero
slope are not in conflict: the slope is estimated precisely from 467 vehicles,
but individual vehicles scatter widely around the line.

That scatter shows up in the intervals at 2000 kg. The confidence interval for
the average vehicle is `r round(mass_ci[, "lwr"], 2)` to
`r round(mass_ci[, "upr"], 2)` L/100 km, but the prediction interval for one
vehicle runs from `r round(mass_pi[, "lwr"], 1)` to `r round(mass_pi[, "upr"], 1)`
L/100 km, nearly twice as wide as the engine-size prediction interval.

```{r}
plot(mass_model, which = 1)
plot(mass_model, which = 2)
plot(mass_model, which = 3)
plot(mass_model, which = 5)

augment(mass_model, data = vehicles) |>
  slice_max(.cooksd, n = 5) |>
  select(make, model, body_type, gross_mass_kg, fuel_use_l_per_100km, .cooksd)
```

**L:** The residual trend is close to flat, with a slight upward bend at high
fitted values; mass alone gives a roughly straight but very noisy mean.
**I:** The same design concern as before: variants of one model share mass and
engines. **N:** This is the main concern. The Q-Q plot bends strongly upwards
in the upper tail: a group of vehicles use far more fuel than their mass
predicts. **E:** The spread is roughly constant across fitted values, although
the large positive residuals make it look uneven.

The residuals are right-skewed, so the symmetric prediction interval at
2000 kg is not trustworthy for one vehicle: its upper limit is probably too low
and its lower limit too high. The largest Cook's distances belong to light,
high-performance sports cars (Lamborghini, McLaren, Porsche) and the heavy
Rolls-Royce Cullinan. None has a large Cook's distance, but the sports cars show
what the model is missing: fuel use depends on what a vehicle's engine is built
for, not just how heavy it is.

Taken together, one numerical vehicle specification can explain a substantial
part of the variation in fuel use, but none of these single-predictor models
predicts every vehicle exactly. Engine size is the strongest of the three
single-predictor summaries here by in-sample $R^2$, followed by power and then
gross mass. Its main limitations are mild curvature for the largest engines,
a heavier upper tail than normal, and dependence between variants of the same
model.


## Looking ahead

One predictor at a time leaves a lot of variation unexplained. Next week we put
several numeric predictors into one model. Each slope then becomes an adjusted
comparison, interpreted with the other predictors held fixed.
